lead: A tree is a connected graph with no cycle. A forest is a collection of trees that do not touch. This one restriction — no cycle — forces a rigid edge count and very simple paths. Trees model folder structures, family trees, decision paths and broadcast networks. They also give the cleanest example of minimal connection: every edge is needed, and no edge is spare. This chapter proves the standard equivalent forms and fixes the vocabulary of rooted trees.
prereq: You need: connectivity and cycles from 6.3, and basic graph terms from 6.1.

sections.h3: Tree definition and four equivalent forms

blocks.text: In a simple graph, a tree T = (V, E) is connected and acyclic. Acyclic means it has no cycle of length 3 or more. A forest is a disjoint union of trees; each component of a forest is a tree. A leaf is a vertex of degree 1. A tree is minimally connected: it is connected, but deleting any edge breaks connectivity.

blocks.where: n is the number of vertices of the tree; m is the number of edges.

blocks.text: Every tree with n > 1 has a leaf. Take a longest simple path v<sub>0</sub>v<sub>1</sub>…v<sub>k</sub> in the tree. The endpoint v<sub>k</sub> has no neighbour outside the path, or the path could be extended. It is not adjacent to any earlier vertex v<sub>i</sub> with i < k − 1, or v<sub>i</sub>v<sub>i+1</sub>…v<sub>k</sub> together with the edge v<sub>k</sub>v<sub>i</sub> would form a cycle. So v<sub>k</sub> has degree 1.

Proof of m = n − 1 by induction on n. For n = 1, m = 0. For n > 1, remove a leaf and its one edge. The rest is still a tree: it stays connected, because no path between two remaining vertices used the leaf, and it stays acyclic, because deleting an edge cannot create a cycle. It has n − 1 vertices and m − 1 edges. By induction m − 1 = (n − 1) − 1, so m = n − 1.

For a simple graph with n vertices, these statements are equivalent: (1) it is a tree; (2) it is connected and has n − 1 edges; (3) it is acyclic and has n − 1 edges; (4) every two vertices are joined by exactly one simple path; (5) adding an edge between two nonadjacent vertices creates exactly one cycle; (6) it is connected, and removing any edge disconnects it (equivalently, every edge is a bridge).

The unique path is the key. If two simple paths joined the same pair, their union would contain a cycle. In a tree, an extra edge between u and v closes the existing u–v path into one cycle. Any other cycle would need a second new edge. Removing an edge on the unique path leaves no alternative route.

A rooted tree chooses one vertex as the root. The root has depth 0. For an edge from a parent to a child, the child is one edge farther from the root. Siblings share the same parent. A vertex with no children is a leaf of the rooted tree; in an unrooted tree with at least two vertices, a leaf has degree 1. The depth of a vertex is the number of edges from the root; the height of the tree is the largest depth. A binary tree is a rooted tree in which every vertex has at most two children.

In the figure, A is root, B and C are children of A. D and E are children of B; F is child of C; G is child of F. D, E and G are leaves. The depths are: A 0, B 1, C 1, D 2, E 2, F 2, G 3. Height is 3.

blocks.where: h is the height of a binary tree in edges; the value is the maximum number of vertices such a binary tree can have.

blocks.text: Rooted trees organise file folders, family records and expression parsing. A spanning tree is a tree that uses all vertices of a graph without a cycle; see 6.9.

A forest with c components can be checked component by component. Suppose the components have n₁, n₂, …, n_c vertices. Component i is a tree, so it has n_i − 1 edges. Adding over all components gives total edges m = Σ(n_i − 1) = n − c.

blocks.where: n is the number of vertices of the forest; m is the number of edges; c is the number of connected components.

blocks.text: For c = 1 this becomes m = n − 1, the tree formula. For c = 3 and n = 12, m = 9, as in the worked example.

The condition “n − 1 edges” alone is not enough. A triangle plus one isolated vertex has n = 4, m = 3, but it is not a tree: it is disconnected and contains a cycle. A connected graph with n − 1 edges is a tree; an acyclic graph with n − 1 edges is also a tree.

Minimal connection has a practical meaning. If vertices are towns and edges are leased fibre links, a tree connects all towns with the fewest links and no backup route. Adding one link gives exactly one cycle, which is the cheapest form of redundancy. A minimum spanning tree finds the cheapest such tree when links have costs; see 6.9.

figure.caption: A rooted tree with seven vertices and six edges; notice n − 1 = 6. Root A has children B and C, and G is a leaf at depth 3.

spec.aria: A rooted tree with root A, children B and C; B has children D and E; C has child F; F has child G. Seven vertices and six edges.

examples.question: A simple graph T has 10 vertices and is a tree. (a) Find the number of edges of T. (b) One new edge is added between two vertices of T that were not adjacent. How many cycles does the new graph contain? (c) A forest F has 12 vertices and 3 components. Find the number of edges of F.
steps: For a tree, m = n − 1. Here n = 10, so m = 10 − 1 = 9 edges.

The two chosen vertices already have exactly one simple path in T. The new edge plus that path forms one cycle. No second cycle can appear because the tree had no cycle and only one edge was added, so the answer is 1 cycle.
For a forest, m = n − c. Here n = 12 and c = 3, so m = 12 − 3 = 9 edges.
examples.answer: The tree has 9 edges, the new graph has exactly 1 cycle, and the forest has 9 edges.
examples.check:
n_tree = 10
m_tree = n_tree - 1
print(m_tree)
print(1)
n_forest = 12
c = 3
m_forest = n_forest - c
print(m_forest)

traps: n − 1 edges alone does not make a tree; the graph must also be connected or acyclic. A triangle plus an isolated vertex has n = 4 and m = 3 but is not a tree.
A forest with c components has n − c edges, not n − 1. The formula n − 1 is only the special case c = 1.
Adding an edge between two existing nonadjacent vertices of a tree creates exactly one cycle, not zero. Adding a new vertex with one edge creates no cycle.
Height is the largest depth in edges, not the number of vertices on the longest path. A one-vertex tree has height 0.

quiz.q: Define a tree and a forest.
quiz.a: A tree is a connected simple graph with no cycle. A forest is a disjoint union of trees.

quiz.q: Why must a tree with n ≥ 1 vertices have n − 1 edges?
quiz.a: Induct on n. For n = 1, m = 0. For n > 1, remove a leaf and its one edge; the remaining tree has n − 1 vertices and m − 1 edges. By induction m − 1 = (n − 1) − 1, so m = n − 1.

quiz.q: A tree has 15 vertices. Find its number of edges.
A simple graph has 8 vertices and 7 edges but is not connected. Can it be a tree? Explain.
quiz.a: No. A tree must be connected. The edge count n − 1 = 7 is necessary but not sufficient. Example: a triangle plus a path on five vertices uses 3 + 4 = 7 edges on 8 vertices and is disconnected.

quiz.q: A forest has 20 vertices and 4 components. Find its number of edges.
What happens when one edge is added between two nonadjacent vertices of a tree?
quiz.a: Exactly one cycle is created, because the tree already has a unique path between those vertices; the new edge closes that path.

quiz.q: Prove that removing any edge from a tree disconnects it.
quiz.a: Let the removed edge be uv. If the remaining graph stayed connected, it would contain a u–v path P not using uv. Then P plus uv is a cycle, contradicting that the original graph is a tree. Hence removal disconnects.

beyond: Not for the exam. Trees lead to treewidth, a measure of how close a graph is to a tree; many hard problems become easy on graphs of small treewidth. Phylogenetic trees organise species by shared ancestry, and parse trees drive compilers. Decision trees in machine learning split data by tests and are read like rooted trees. Search terms: treewidth, phylogenetic tree, parse tree, decision tree, union–find forest.
